description: Grip a broom by the end and lift it to horizontal with one hand. How far from the end you can grip exposes the truth about your forearm tendons: they are cables working a lever, and leverage never lies. Here is the physics, the bands, and the training.

lines: Slide your grip until you find your truth.
beats.title: THE LEVER TEST

beats.text: SLOW LIFT, NO SWING, NO JERK

scenes.narration: Take your broom and hold it out to the side of its head, so the handle points behind you like a tail. Grip the very end with one hand, arm down, then slowly lift the broom with your wrist and forearm until the handle is horizontal, head high behind you, using nothing but the lever strength of your forearm. Too hard? Slide your grip a few centimeters toward the head and try again. Keep sliding until you find the closest point to the end where you can lift it clean, hold it level for three seconds, and lower it under control. Measure the centimeters between your grip and the end of the handle. That distance is your score. Smaller is stronger. Got your centimeters, both arms? Keep them. At the end of this video I will tell you the truth they reveal about your forearm tendons.

lines: Every centimeter is a pay cut for the load.
beats.title: THE CM RULE

scenes.label: CENTIMETERS FROM THE END OF THE HANDLE
scenes.narration: Here is the line, and it runs backwards from every other test this season: smaller wins. Ten centimeters from the end is a trained forearm. Beyond twenty, the lever system is untrained, and untrained is fixable. At zero, gripping the very end and levering the broom clean, you own a forearm that strongmen and old-school physical culturists have chased for a century, because this test cannot be cheated with momentum, body English, or a good day. The broom's weight never changes. Only your distance from its balance point changes, and each centimeter you slide inward cuts the load your tendons must beat. Hold your centimeters. Now the truth, because this simple broom is about to explain your entire forearm better than any machine in any gym.
scenes.sub: over 20 cm: untrained levers - 0 cm: elite forearm tendons

lines: Long lever outside it. Physics wins ties.
beats.title: THE UNFAIR LEVER

beats.text: TENDONS PULL CENTIMETERS FROM THE JOINT

scenes.narration: Look at the machine you are testing. Your wrist tendons do not attach far from the joint. They cross within a centimeter or two of the wrist's center, which gives them a very short internal lever. The broom's head pulls on a lever over a meter long. Do the quiet math and the broom's modest weight becomes an enormous tension demand inside your forearm: the cables must pull with many times the broom's weight just to hold the geometry still. This is the truth about forearm tendons that the mirror never shows. They are not built for showy peak force. They are built to win unfair leverage battles, all day, at terrible mechanical disadvantage, without tearing. When you lever that broom, you are reading the exact quality they evolved for. And because the disadvantage is fixed by your anatomy, the only way the number improves is the cable itself getting stronger and stiffer. There is nowhere to hide. That is why this test is a classic.

beats.title: CM FROM THE END BY TRAINING

lines: Same broom. Same weight. Different tendon.
beats.title: THE HONEST SCALE

scenes.narration: Here is why old-school strongmen loved levering and modern gyms forgot it. Most strength tests can be gamed a little: a bounce here, a swing there, a friendly judge. A lever cannot. The load is fixed by geometry, the fulcrum is your own wrist, and the tape measure reads the verdict in centimeters that do not flatter anyone. This is also why lever strength transfers so strangely well to real life. The world hands you unfair levers constantly: a wrench at the end of its handle, a full pan grabbed by its grip, a suitcase lifting away from your body, a door swinging on its hinge. Every one of them is your forearm tendons against a long lever and a short internal one. Men who train levers develop a kind of strength that surprises people in workshops and kitchens, because daily life is a lever festival and almost nobody trains for it. Your centimeters are a direct quote of your real-world forearm. No translation needed.

beats.text: THE REVERSE LEVER FINDS THE EXTENSORS
A COMPLETE FOREARM LEVERS BOTH WAYS

scenes.narration: Now the deep cut: the lever has a second direction, and it grades the other cable team. Flip the broom so the head hangs low in front of you and lever it up the other way, and the work moves from the flexor side of the forearm to the extensor side, the same opening system from the finger spread test, now under real load. Most men discover a gap here you could drive through: strong lifting the first way, helpless in reverse. That gap matters, because the two teams share one wrist, and the wrist performs at the level of its weaker crossing. A complete forearm levers both directions at similar distances. Test the reverse with the same rules, slow lift, three-second hold, centimeters from the end, and write down both numbers. If they differ wildly, you have just been handed your training program by a broom: the reverse direction gets priority until the two scores shake hands.

And the skinny advantage in the lever test is that there is barely a disadvantage to overcome. The broom's lever does not lengthen because a bigger man picks it up, and the internal lever in a lean wrist is the same few centimeters as in a thick one. What separates scores is tendon quality and the nervous system's willingness to produce enormous tension in a small joint, and both are pure training. Slim forearms even read the test more honestly: less tissue between the tape and the truth. The strongman era understood this. Levering feats were historically dominated not by the heaviest men but by forearm specialists, wiry men whose cables were built for exactly this unfair fight. That is your tribe. The broom is waiting.
Now lever with me. Five slow lifts at your tested grip point, three seconds up, three seconds down, no swing. Feel the cable win the geometry. Go.

beats.text: -1 CM WHEN THE SET IS CLEAN

scenes.narration: Here is your week. Three lever sessions, spaced out, three sets of five slow lifts per arm at your tested grip point, exactly like the block we just did: three seconds up, a three-second hold at horizontal, three seconds down. Momentum is theft; a swung lift trains your ability to swing, not your tendons. Every other session, train the reverse lever at its own grip point until its centimeters approach the front side's. When all three sets are clean at your current distance, slide one centimeter farther out. One. The lever multiplies small changes, so respect the small steps. If the wrist joint itself complains, slide inward and slow down, and see a professional if it persists. In thirty days, retest both directions. Expect the number to move in centimeters and your real-world grip to move in ways that surprise you at odd moments: jars, tools, doors, pans. Leverage is everywhere. Now you are training for it.

So, your lever truth. Beyond twenty centimeters: you are not weak, you are unwired, and you own the most honest room for improvement in the forearm. Ten to twenty: the cables are working, and the slow lifts will walk you outward month by month. Under ten, or zero at the very end: your forearm tendons are genuinely elite, winning the unfair fight your anatomy sets for them every day. Whatever your centimeters are, test both directions, grade the worse one, and remember it is a measurement of one trainable system, not a grade on you. Drop your centimeters in the comments, just the number. Retest in thirty days, same broom, same rules, no swing. Physics is patient. Be as patient as physics, and the tape will move.
Same broom, same rules, thirty days from now: that is the retest. If this way of training makes sense to you, subscribe, because we test a new cable every episode. This is {channel}. Train the cable.

title: Your Wrist Lever Record Reveals the Truth About Your forearm tendons
